Earth's Moon. Our planet's only natural satellite, orbiting at an average distance of three hundred eighty-four thousand four hundred kilometers. It is the fifth-largest moon in the solar system and the only celestial body beyond Earth to have been visited by humans.

The Moon formed approximately four point five billion years ago, likely from a giant impact between Earth and a Mars-sized body called Theia. It has a diameter of three thousand four hundred seventy-four kilometers, and its mass is about one eighty-first of Earth's. The Moon has no atmosphere or magnetic field of its own.

The most striking thing about our Moon is that it is the only moon ever walked on by humans. Twelve astronauts set foot on the lunar surface during the Apollo missions between nineteen sixty-nine and nineteen seventy-two. The Moon is synchronously rotating, always showing the same face to Earth because its rotation period equals its orbital period of approximately twenty-seven point three days.

The Moon's surface is dominated by highlands, which are ancient and light-colored, and by maria, which are darker volcanic plains that are younger. The surface is heavily cratered. In two thousand nine, orbital spectroscopy discovered water ice in permanently shadowed craters, transforming lunar science. The Moon's gravitational influence regulates Earth's tides and stabilizes our planet's axial tilt. Without it, ocean tides would be negligible and Earth's axial tilt would be unstable.
